utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you taken as prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who took you as prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Approximately, when were you captured, can you remember, or taken prisoner, can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 20th October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once you were taken prisoner, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to the detention in Hrasnica and that is where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is at Hrasnica? What is there? What is at this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is this an army base of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did they keep you at Hrasnica for, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About one month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From where did you go after you left Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you still kept as a prisoner when you were brought to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where in Sarajevo were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to the Security Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you remember, approximately, what date you arrived at the Security Centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. It was in January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Before you were captured in October 1994 and during the period you were held prisoner up until January 1995, had you heard whether or not Dusko Tadic -- what had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever watch television while you were in Prijedor during '93, '94 and when you were in the army camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever read anything in the newspaper during this time about what had happened to Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were captured by the army, by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they question you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did they ask you about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked me about my arrival in the army, where was I, what army did I belong in, where did I go to do my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you asked about the Trnopolje camp and what you had done there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was it that asked you this? Was it the Security Centre people or was it the military people at Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked me at the Security Centre or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was the name Dusko Tadic first brought up in this interrogation, in these interrogations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Previously, they asked me if I knew Dusko Tadic, whether I had ever seen him, and I told them that I had been receiving humanitarian aid in Kozarac and that I knew Dusko Tadic and that I had seen him in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in Sarajevo were a number of statements taken from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you then subsequently charged with having committed (redacted) contrary to the law of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you plead guilty to this charge and admit that you had committed the crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you told by the Court that you would be treated as a minor because at the time you committed the crimes you were under age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you told that the maximum sentence that you could be given was a period of imprisonment for 10 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For how many years were you sentenced to imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you represented at the time by a Defence lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many years left have you got to serve of that (redacted) sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Has anyone offered you any inducements or promises or favours in exchange for you giving evidence in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would just like to take you back, if I may, to have a look at some Exhibits for me and tell me whether or not you recognise the photographs that I am showing. Might the witness be shown firstly Exhibit 310? Witness, could you look at that photograph for me, please, and tell me if you recognise the building that you see there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where is the school, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did that school form part of the camp at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the school which is in what was the camp ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps they could just be put on to the screen so we can see? Thank you. Might that be, that Exhibit be returned to the Registrar and could the witness be please shown Exhibit 304? Just looking at Exhibit 304, witness, can you tell me what that is a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, what school is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Trnopolje school from the -- which faces Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps that could be placed on the screen? Might the Exhibit be returned to the Registrar? Would you look now for me, please, at Exhibit 303? Do you recognise the building that is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What building is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The co-operative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where is that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did that building form part of the camp at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that photograph be returned to the Registrar and might the witness be shown Exhibit 302? Witness, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is it a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depicts the road from Kozarac to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would ask you to put that on the screen and point to something for me. Thank you. Just on the machine itself, not on the television set, can you point to the direction of Kozarac on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated on the photograph] This is the direction towards Kozarac and then you come to this cross section -- sorry, do you have to hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. You need to try to point to it and then speak into the microphone, if you can. So point to it, just hold the pointer there and then tell us what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here is the asphalt towards Kozarac, to the railway station. This road is towards Prijedor. To the right is towards Omarska. What you see here, this is the transformer substation and there is a shed. Not far from the shed is dom, the co-operative, and from it you can see part of the school, as you can see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As you are coming down the road from Kozarac towards the railway station in Trnopolje, is the co-operative building and the school on your right-hand side or your left-hand side, as you come from Kozarac down the road to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You have just referred for the first time in the last few minutes to the co-operative building which was much referred to in evidence. Is that the same as the dom?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: [To the witness]: The white house that you spoke of where many of the prisoners were taken, as you come down the road from Kozarac towards the railway station at Trnopolje, is that on the right-hand side or on the left-hand side of the road as you come down from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Might that photograph be returned. As far as you know, what was the nationality or ethnic group of the prisoners and the young girls that were taken out of the camp and either murdered or raped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were of Muslim nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Earlier in your evidence, I think yesterday in your evidence, you described a building as having one storey. By that description how many floors do you mean by "one storey"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ground floor and one floor, upper floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Also in your evidence yesterday you referred to sideburns being the shape of someone's hair on their head. What is your understanding of sideburns in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a man whose hair is receding on the sides of his forehead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, I now ask you, if you would please, to look around the courtroom and tell me if you see the person that you know and recognise as Dusko Tadic that you saw at this camp in Trnopolje and in the building in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The person you are pointing to, would you please describe where he sits in the courtroom and the clothes that he has on, as best you can see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is sitting on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe the clothes that he has on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is wearing civilians clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What colour is his coat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He has a blue coat, a jacket sorry. He has a shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the record reflect, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, the record will reflect that the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell me if you have ever given any interviews to the television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Or to the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you been interviewed by anyone other than those you have told us about in Sarajevo and elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina concerning these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be on television?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have told us about being interviewed by the Security Police in Bosnia-Herzegovina and by lawyers in Sarajevo. Have any other people interviewed you about these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You are quite sure you have not spoken to anyone from a newspaper, a journalist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were arrested by the troops of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were at that time wounded, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What company of the army of the Republika Srpska were you serving with at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Lordship, may I say it or do I not say it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like you to identify the unit you were in at the time that you were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just excuse me a second. No, we consider the witness ought to answer the question, your Honour. We do not wish to make an objection. We do not wish to raise any objection to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Witness, you should respond to the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall I repeat it, your Honour, as I might be able to express it rather more clearly than I did before? [To the witness]: Can you describe to me the name of the unit you were serving in at the time that you were arrested by the troops of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First Motorized Guard Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where is the base of the First Motorized Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karlinovik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Had you served in that Brigade during your time of mobilization with the Republika Srpska Army exclusively, or had you been in any other Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the only Brigade I served with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was your rank in the Brigade and what work were you involved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no rank. I was just a private on the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you in the infantry or in any other unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Infantry. Infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you joined the infantry for the First Brigade on what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the 12th July '94.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you joined that Brigade did you have your military book with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I had left it in Karlinovik in the military barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were the details of your service in the Brigade entered in your military book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In July 1994 how old were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were captured by the troops of Bosnia-Herzegovina, how old were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had not turned 19 yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object, your Honour. I do object to that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is the basis for the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Order itself.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Identifying characteristic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Identifying characteristic, your Honour. Once the precise date of birth becomes known, it is our submission that the process of tracking down and locating this person and who his parents are becomes much more easy. In relation to that, your Honour, the decision of the Chamber in relation to that specifically says on page 7, when your Honours refer to this you say: "The Prosecutor has explained that the kind of identifying data concerning witness L which the Prosecutor has sought to withhold from the Defence is the Witness L's date of birth, his parents' names and address and his previous address and such like." Your Honours then go on and make a general order about identifying data. In my submission, your Honours, it encompasses that. Date of birth is a very specific and important piece of identifying data that can be relied on for that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay? You are smiling. I guess that is what it says in the Order!

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What else would you like me to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is a long order.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is the standard language that is contained in the Orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We know this witness's name.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As that has been disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Through the procedure that has been utilized.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. He has given considerable detail about where he was staying in the Prijedor region. I am concerned, because we challenge his evidence, to look at what he has to say about himself, where he has been. I am particularly concerned about the information that he was too young to be charged in relation to these matters by the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina because he was a minor. As I understand it, he was certainly 18 in 1994 and some of these offences could have been committed at an age of 17, and whether that constitutes the status of a minor within that jurisdiction in relation to these offences we are concerned with.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would not the decision of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Court indicate whether he was to be treated as a minor and whether they were right or wrong having made that determination, is that not sufficient for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would certainly like to consider what has been said about that. We have been given no access to any information about this witness, although we have striven to prepare the defence in relation to what ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Well, the Order is the Order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You did not object. Judge Stephen wants to say something and perhaps Judge Vohrah. Judge Stephen says a month is enough for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I do not quibble with that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is a month enough for you to determine whether he is a minor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is something I would certainly like to consider and if I was given a month it would help me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It would help you, but would it help you to determine whether he is a minor? That is what you want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May I be frank? I know already from the statement that I have been given, because it is referred to in that and it is slightly artificial, as far as I am concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Order is the Order and it says "date of birth", a month. Then you say you want it because you want to know whether he is a minor and giving the month is not going to tell you whether he is a minor. Then you tell me you have it in the statement. So I will sustain the objection of Mr. Niemann. The date of birth is precluded from the Order. Judge Stephen dissents because ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I dissent because the date of birth is not in question.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is not in question but it is in the Order, so we have to stand by the Order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. May I explain myself a little bit fully on this, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You want the witness to take off his earphones?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. L, would you please take off your earphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is also after 1 o'clock and perhaps if we were able to discuss the matter amongst ourselves we might be able to find a way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: With the Prosecutor you really should discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because it is in the Order. The Prosecutor asks the Tribunal to stand by the Order. We cannot deviate from our Order, that is for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you wanted to know whether he was a minor you need his date of birth. So I do not know how we are going to do deal with it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not know the precise date of birth because of the month that these offences are committed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You need the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They range from October to December. He has already told us that he was 18 in 1994. So I know where I am going on this.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you need the year of his birth?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will not need it in relation to -- because we know that he was 18 in 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will let Counsel talk. You talk amongst each other and then we will stand in recess. Talk with the Prosecutor and let us see what we can do for you to satisfy your concern, as well as not impeach our own Order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (2.30 p.m.) PRIVATE

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, before you call in witness L, let us see if we have resolved that matter regarding the date of birth for L. So we will not have to ask him to take his earphones off, he is not present. What have you, lawyers, done? I sure hope you have worked it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have not resolved it in the way I think that the Defence would like us to resolve it, but what we have done is gathered up some material to assist the Court and the Defence on this issue, because I think the question of whether or not he was dealt with as a minor or otherwise relates to the law of Yugoslavia. We have that material available to give to the Court. Your Honours, he has already given in testimony that in October 1992 he was 16 years of age and then in October 1994 he was 18 years of age. According to the law of former Yugoslavia, in relation to treatment of minors, a person between the ages of 16 and 18 years of age is considered to be a senior minor. The maximum imprisonment that can be imposed on a senior minor for an offence is a period of not more than 10 years imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is the date on the decision? When did the Court in Bosnia consider that he was a minor? Of course, we have looked at the decision that we entered in November and we can tell you about that, but give me that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I do not think I have that particular date here, your Honour. I have a letter from the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina stating that the High Court of Sarajevo had conducted criminal proceedings against L. They go on to say: "Since an under age individual is in question and, in accordance with our criminal proceedings, the identity of this individual has not been disclosed in public".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is the date on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is a letter of 2nd November 1995 which is later in '95, but my understanding is that sentence was imposed upon him in the first half of 1995. I am not sure what date that was, but I can endeavour to find that out. This letter also goes on to say: "Our criminal proceedings code requires the under age individual charged with criminal offences to be protected and their identity unrevealed and, therefore, we would like to ask you to maintain both his name and other personal data confidential". Then there is attached to this letter some extracts from their law, some of it appearing in the Serbo-Croatian language, but other of it having been translated. I am dealing with those matters raised in the letter, but no reference is made to the date of the sentence. The provision relating to the law is summarised in a special report that was prepared for the Tribunal in relation to sentencing practices in the law of former Yugoslavia. That is, in fact, a summary of the provisions which I have also extracted which does require a reading of a number of provisions to get to the position which is summarised in the sentencing practice. One needs to read Articles 66 and 79, 79(C) and 79(D) of those provisions in order to see the actual provisions which are summarised. So, if your Honours please, I hand up a copy of the letter from the government of Sarajevo and could a copy of that, please, be given to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before we even get to that, what does our decision of November, say, regarding the confidentiality of the proceedings in Bosnia-Herzegovina? In paragraph 2, at least, of the decision it says: "Witness L was employed as a guard in Trnopolje camp in which capacity he committed serious crimes for which he has been convicted by a Court in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a trial of which neither the proceedings nor the decision have been made public because he was tried as a minor". Are you now making public a portion of those proceedings, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. No. I am specifically not doing that. What I am doing is making available a copy of the letter which does not contain the proceedings themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Back to the date of birth of the witness. Mr. Kay, you have a statement of the witness, I gather?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And his date of birth was not redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, his date of the birth was in that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That the Prosecutor gave you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not sure that is -- I do not understand this. The statement was redacted, as I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It refers to his birthday and returning home on his birthday.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The decision in paragraph 8 on page 12 says: "No identifying data concerning witness L, other than his name and position at Trnopolje camp and the time taken for travel by witness L from his residence to the camp shall be disclosed to the defence counsel or to the accused, and the names, addresses, whereabouts of, and other identifying data concerning witness L's relatives shall not be disclosed to the defence counsel or to the accused". That would seem to cover his date of birth. So we are back with the same problem, I guess, unless you can give us some help, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It just requires 2 plus 2 -- the paragraph starts with a particular date, and then later on after the narrative it refers to a birthday and so the connection is obvious.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are talking about the statement, back to the decision of the Trial Chamber regarding the release to the accused of the date of birth? Once again the decision seems to prohibit that. In paragraph 17, on page 8: "The defence counsel and the accused will know the name of witness L; that witness L will be present to testify in person; that the Judges, defence counsel and the accused will be able to observe the demeanour of witness L; and that the Defence will be given the opportunity of cross-examinining witness L on his evidence except with regard to matters which may result in the names and whereabouts of members of his family being revealed". What you now want to ask the witness is his date of birth and that is an objection that has been raised and sustained?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Where are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I assist the Court ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- because Mr. Niemann led evidence that he was 16 when he started working at the camp in October. I want to make the next step in the next month, which is all I am seeking to do, to establish his date of birth -- his age, not his date of birth, his age, when we are dealing with the events in November and December. As the Prosecution have led the age for the start of his work at the camp in October, I cannot really see what the problem is in relation to his age in November and December, if it is different from that in October.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you will then ask him his age at a particular point in time and not his date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I intended to give him the month of November and say, "Are you aged 17 during that month?"

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann? That was not the question that you asked before. I think you asked the date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, now everything has come down on top of me .....

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The decision, for one. Mr. Niemann, what Mr. Kay says is that you asked him what was his age in October 1992. Actually, he said: "Were you not 16 in October 1992?" and he answered. Then now what Mr. Kay says is he wants to ask him, "Well, how old were you in another particular month?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We have no objection to a question, "How old were you in November 1992?"

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that the question, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, that is all I seek.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is very good. I wish you had only sought that before our lunch break, then I would not have had to dig this decision out to take a look at it! Then if there is no objection, then that question will be allowed, but keep in mind once again that you will not get the date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, and I am not concerned ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If there is any concern on the part of the Prosecutor that any of this information that has been elicited regarding the witness's age should be redacted from the transcript that goes out, then that is something the Prosecutor needs to consider. That is something, I am sure, that the witness unit will consider before the transcript goes out. That is another matter though. That really does relate to what Mr. Kay wishes to elicit at this point. OK. Fine. There is no objection. Bring in Mr. L, please. WITNESS L, recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, how long do you anticipate that you will need to complete cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think I will be the afternoon, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you think you will finish by 5.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am hopeful, I cannot promise it, but I know that the proceedings are on course to finish by the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are hoping to finish on Thursday actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think there is a good chance.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Good, thank you. Cross-examined by MR. KAY, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may be seated and we are still in closed session. Mr. Kay, you may continue with cross-examination. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am much obliged, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness, is it right that in November 1992 you were 17 years of age?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You should answer the question, sir, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not fully 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For the most part of November 1992, were you 17 years of age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You told the Court that after you left Trnopolje camp you went into hiding for 10 days in opstina Prijedor, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not think that is a correct recital of the evidence. He went into hiding outside of opstina Prijedor. I have not checked the transcript. It may be that the transcript does not read that way, but that was certainly my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is my note and I will be able to deal with this, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Outside of opstina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I was not really interested in this portion of the evidence but...

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After 10 days of being in hiding, did you return to opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There you told us that you remained for one and a half years before joining the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say you returned to opstina Prijedor, which part of opstina Prijedor did you return to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kozarac, Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You say that you were in hiding from Bosko Dragicevic and policemen who were looking for you, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you were in Kozarac for that length of time, did you not move around, did you not walk around, did people not know that you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What about the people that were friends of yours, fellow refugees that you have told us about, did they know you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because Kozarac at that time did not have many people living in the village, did it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- I must object to questions about where the witness was at these particular times in the particular towns. His evidence was that he returned to the Kozarac, Trnopolje area. The questioning since that moment has been continually concentrating on Kozarac. The witness has not said he was at Kozarac. I object to any question which either suggests he was at Kozarac or that may be inferred that he is at that place.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is the basis for the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Because, your Honours, in my submission, it leads to ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are you saying it is misleading or that that is not what the witness testified, or are you saying that it would violate the November order granting protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am saying it violates the order granting protective measures in that it provides information relating to a previous address.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And it may result in the names and whereabouts of members of his family being revealed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It could well do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do not mean to cause difficulties because, as the Court can see, I am trying to cross-examine. I did have this information in a statement which is how I was able to discount one place and put to him that it was Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you are saying that the Prosecutor waived?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was a statement disclosed to the Defence and it is an area of evidence with which I am ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why do you not have the statement marked for identification purposes and offer the statement? If you have been given it, and we are now trying to get into areas which, at least, the Prosecutor claims would be objectionable, if you have been given it, it seems to me the argument may be that they have waived this request. Of course, I do not know whether that will get past our order granting their request, but if you have it in the statement, why do you not offer the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours provided a solution there and if I mark it, it may be of help.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor may have an objection, but we will hear it, but that is their problem. If they give you the information, then they have given it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I am not meaning to cause them difficulties.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No. You are cross-examining. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you want that marked? Is that what you want to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am just doing it now, your Honour, yes. The statement is in English when I look at it and there is no Serbo-Croat of this statement which was later disclosed to us. I will see what I can do. Witness, I would like you to look at this statement which was, apparently, a statement made by you which I tender as D33.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Get the witness to identify his signature on the statement, that he can do, whether it is English or Serbo-Croat, and then you read the statement and then we have the benefit of interpretation and the witness can then hear your interpretation. The Prosecutor can check the English version to make sure you are reading it correctly. Do you want to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Everything has been crossed out on the statement, your Honour, including his signature. It has just got "L" at the top of the page. Unless someone on the other side of the courtroom has got an original without these matters redacted, it is the statement dated 4th April 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Maybe we can go to another area and then at the recess we will see what we can do with the statement, if that will help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. [To the witness]: Perhaps if you would just look at that page where there is a yellow highlight? Perhaps if the statement would be handed back to me, I will provide the witness with the place. Thank you. Witness, you will see highlighted in yellow with a blue circle the name of a place in opstina Prijedor. Is that the place where you stayed for one and a half years -- do not say the name of the place, but just agree or disagree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could the statement be handed back to me, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you ever said that you stayed in that place before joining the army in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I apologise, but can I ask the honourable Judges something about Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you want to ask whether or not you should reveal this -- we still have not resolved that problem yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I know, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The order does say that even the Defence is not to be provided with information that may result in the identification of the names and whereabouts of members of family. Is that the area that we are getting into?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It seems that we are, your Honours. I am interested in this one and a half years that the witness spends in the area of opstina Prijedor. I think the Court realises that this is not a particularly big area, and that the identification of this place will not provide any lesser means of being able to identify this witness's family. We are dealing with a locality that the Court is very well aware of people's relations, how they know each other pretty well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So what are you saying, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That in me being restrained in being able to put in precise terms the place name to this witness so that I can adequately develop proper questions is probably an unnecessary restriction, given the fact that this has been disclosed to the Defence in this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the reference to the place in the statement that has been drawn to the attention of the witness, there has been evidence that that place, Kozarac, is an area larger than the centre of that place. It seems to me that if there are questions about, was it that area, then we have no objection to that. We do have objections if it goes beyond that into particulars of where in that particular place it was, because Kozarac is a large area, including Trnopolje, because the railway station itself in Trnopolje is called the Kozarac railway station.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The order would prevent the revelation of that information to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So to the extent that we, as a Chamber, have an obligation to enforce the order, then I would sustain the objection. To the extent that the Prosecutor has already given you the information outside of the Trial Chamber's involvement, that is a matter, I suppose, between the two of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But if it goes beyond the name of the witness, the time that it took for him to travel from his home to the camp, the order just seems to be very clear on that. I do not know what to do, Mr. Kay, other than to prohibit you from getting into that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I am actually having a bit of difficulty here trying to develop the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I mean the order is pretty clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May the Defence confer, your Honour, to see?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sure. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. My learned friend Mr. Wladimiroff has referred me to the original order which was concerned with prejudice. This information has been disclosed to us subsequently by the Prosecution. The evidence that was given relating to these matters after the witness had left the camp is new evidence to us and material that we had no knowledge of before it was given before this Court. It is an area with which we are concerned to question because this evidence is challenged, and the credibility of the witness is challenged. So, we feel it is only right, given the fact that this is a closed session, that there may be editing of the transcripts of these proceedings before they are released to the general public, that no prejudice is occasioned to the witness or the Prosecution if we do go into these matters in more detail than we are permitted to at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it depends on just how far the Defence wish to go into this line of questioning. We do not want to be seen or to be unnecessarily restricting their cross-examination on these matters. I do not understand fully what they mean by this being new information, but it seems to me that with the opportunity to do redacting before it is made public, a lot of our problems may be allayed. But we are concerned, very concerned, about questioning which leads to or could lead to the identification of the witness's family.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Judge Vohrah can speak for himself, but what he has pointed out to me is that what is at issue here is really the protection of the witness, not the Prosecutor. There has been a promise made to the witness, and that the Prosecutor cannot waive that right, and perhaps through inadvertence or mistake, or however it occurred, they give information to the Defence that is contrary to the order, then that should not enure to the detriment of the witness, because that is what this order is all about really, is protecting the witness, not the Prosecutor. The order really goes to withholding information from the Defence regarding the identity, not the public. I looked at another decision of witness S that we were focusing on, and then that was withholding only from the public, but this is focusing on withholding from the Defence because of a fear of retaliation -- pure and simple. So that does not solve it, the fact that it may be redacted when it goes out to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Our difficulty here is in representing the defendant and challenging the evidence in the interests ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The order, as you will have to look at the decision itself, says that it was not objected to except certain matters, but at this point ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My learned leader who dealt with these pleadings.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, if your Honour pleases, in paragraph 15 of your decision, your Chamber said: "In order to establish whether the restriction on his right to examine or have examined a witness against him is in accordance with the notion of a fair trial, this Trial Chamber must balance the interests of the accused and those of witness L". Then it goes on to explain why the balance struck, as it did, your decision because you considered that no such prejudice has been shown to exist in this case -- I may add "at that moment". After this decision, we got three more statements from the Prosecution and then the issue was raised. So what I am trying to say here is that this problem has arisen, we feel that, indeed, we are limited in the right to have the witness examined. Therefore, we suggest that you reconsider on the basis of this new information provided to the Defence that the balance may strike at another point.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the provision of further information to the Defence about the matters should not be, in my submission, used as a basis upon which the Defence can seek to go around the Court's order. The additional information given to the Defence is for the benefit of the Defence, not for them to use it as a basis on which they can undermine the Court's order. The Court's order has been made. The Prosecution has certainly obligations that it has to fulfil and to make certain judgments with respect to material that it is in possession of. It is also under certain obligations with respect to the Rules of the Tribunal. When an assessment is made of all these matters, the Prosecutor can and does reveal information to the Defence. In so doing, it is not sought in any way to go behind an order of the court or to undermine it. It is merely to provide the Defence with information so as to assist them in their course. It is not, in my submission, an appropriate or valid basis upon which to argue that the order is no longer in place or that it should be ignored. If the additional information does not assist the Defence, then they may return it, keep it or do with it what they like. But it was given to them for that purpose and for no other purpose, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The problem though is, your Honour, that if the further information reveals inconsistency and, therefore, founds a basis for cross-examination dealing with reliability, we feel we should not be restricted if, indeed, a fair trial is at stake here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If that be the case, your Honour, perhaps we might be assisted by the Defence telling us whether or not the inconsistencies relate to matter which go to identify the witness or the witness's family. I mean, there may well be material there which they may argue amounts to a basis upon which it can be argued that there are inconsistencies. If those inconsistencies go to the question of matters pertaining to the identification of the witness or the witness's family or their residence or whatever, then let us consider it on that basis. But we have heard nothing of this sort. The questions of inconsistencies may well relate to other matters entirely of which there is no limitation whatsoever on the Defence in their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, what are the areas of you wish to enquire? Can you just for the record specify those areas without -- you are not going to address the defendant (sic), but I would like you to make an offer really, a proof, in a sense of what is it that you would want to elicit? Do you want the witness to take his -- yes, please, would you take your earphones off? Let me explain. Would you put your earphones back on? [To the witness]: Sir, it is not our intention to deny you the full opportunity to be a part of this proceeding, but there are certain matters that the lawyers wish to discuss that raise legal issues. Those legal issues need to be resolved without your hearing the underlying discussion, but we are not attempting to just keep you uninformed. It is just that we are now discussing legal issues that need to be resolved first before we continue with your testimony. So that is why I am asking you to take off your earphones, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, what are the areas you would want to get into?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am just looking at a statement here that reads: "I performed the guard duty in Trnopolje camp until 28th December 1992 when I left the place at my own request". Moving on: "I heard from the aforementioned guards and military policemen that Tadic had gone to his wife in Serbia and had not return to Kozarac". It seems to me that the first statement contradicts the leaving of the place and fleeing as described because it implies it was at his own request.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me deal with that. Do you have an objection to that, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, that is one, no objection to. What else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The second statement: "I heard from the aforementioned guards and military policemen that Tadic had gone to his wife in Serbia and had not returned to Kozarac" implies that this witness had association with other people in the area and was able to talk to them about matters, and rather contradicts him being in hiding or trying to escape from the clutches of Bosko Dragicevic and the other policemen which was his testimony this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you ask him then what is the basis for that belief as opposed to asking him, "Well, were you in Kozarac?" because if you ask him if he is in Kozarac, then that is when there is going to be an objection. Can you ask him what is the basis of it? Of course, if he then answers, "I was in Kozarac", that does not help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One of the difficulties is developing it and then exploring issues.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am not trying to run your case really, you are a better lawyer than I am. I have the easier job, that is for sure. I just sit up here and give you my opinion about things. But I am trying to give you as to what you want, but keep in mind that we have this order. So you are saying that you cannot assess the weight that statement should be given unless you find out where he was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and the 18-month period that he is in the opstina Prijedor region or the Kozarac area and what he did with himself and whom he associated with and how, would be of importance to assess -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is a statement, that may be new information. I do not know whether that was in the first statement, or is that in a statement that you received subsequent to the November order?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is a statement dated 19th January 1995 that we received last week.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. But that does not reveal his whereabouts, so that would not be a waiver. That just goes to the information that is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think the names of the people and the particular identities will inevitably focus on the whereabouts of the witness and who he associated with.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will sustain the Prosecution's objection as to that second area, that is, if you are going to ask him with respect to him having heard that Tadic had gone back to Kozarac, if you are going to attempt to ask him his whereabouts, then it seems to me that you are then treading on the November order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, it is the particular guards and policemen who spoke to him from whom he heard this information and how he came to talk to them which would be of interest to us in relation to his credibility. His evidence this morning was that he was in hiding and he was escaping from Bosko Dragicevic and the military policemen because he deserted from the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you not elicit that information without asking where he was residing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it is virtually impossible, your Honour, to do justice to the subject, if I can put it that way. I mean that in a different sense than it might otherwise be construed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. I am trying to give you something, at the same time keep in mind the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you feel you cannot thread through the order and not elicit his whereabouts and at the same time determine what were his sources for this information, then you say you cannot, but you should not elicit his whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think if I ask the sources, the witness will inevitably be giving the information.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because he could have talked to these people in Banja Luka, it does not mean that he spoke to them where he was residing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not know what to tell you other than we will stand by paragraph 17 of the decision in November, and that is that Defence counsel -- I do not need to repeat it and, particularly, paragraph 8 of the disposition section. It is really focusing on the whereabouts of the accused. That is our only intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There was another area I was going to go into which concerned his job. He mentioned working and again ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is that area now, because Mr. Niemann did not object to your first area so we may be able to resolve this if you make your proffer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is not an inconsistent statement but I was going to cross-examine him in relation to where that work was and then, by definition almost, seek to find out if that was an area where Bosko Dragicevic and the others would have been.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We do not have any objection with regards to that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No objection to that. You got two out of three. Do you have anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am sort of launching the boat, your Honour, at the moment and trying to get on it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The order is here and the decision is here. I am sure you have looked at it over the recess -- we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are those your only concerns now, the three areas that you have raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will try to be very careful in how I question. I am very mindful of the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am trying to make you make your proffer, rule on it, to protect the record. You have made a proffer of three points and there has been no objection to two of them. It is only the second one that I have granted Mr. Niemann's objection on. So you may proceed. [To the witness]: Sir, would you put your earphones on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the one and a half years that you were back in the opstina Prijedor, you told the Court this morning that you were working. Whereabouts was that work?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Agriculture, Orlovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Does that mean you were working on a farm in Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that work during the day?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you travel to that work? Did you walk or go on a bus or were you driven in a car?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: It varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Orlovci is very close to Kozarac, is it not? It is in between Kozarac and Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you travel openly to the farm in Orlovci where you were working?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Excuse me, what do you mean, "openly"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So that other people could see you?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Well, everybody passes by, everybody can be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, Orlovci is a place, as you know, which has a checkpoint on the Prijedor/Banja Luka highway, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: There was not one in my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you pass through to Orlovci on the Prijedor/Banja Luka highway?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell me how long the journey was from your place where you were living to the farm at Orlovci where you were working?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I cannot be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long would it take in a motor car?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I did not measure it. I did not look at a watch to see how long it could take.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, but surely you have some idea of time. You are able to tell me whether it took 10 minutes, 15 minutes or 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: It depended. If I started early, I got there earlier. If I started later, then I had to hurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The farm that you worked at, was it on the north side of the Prijedor/Banja Luka highway or was it on the south side, on the Trnopolje side of the highway?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: In the northern and the southern part, in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you work in the fields there or did you work in a building?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: In the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So anyone who knew you, would they be able to see you there at work in the field?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If the farm was on both sides of the Prijedor/Banja Luka highway, are you sure that you did not travel along that highway to get to the farm?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not pass through any checkpoint that the police had at Orlovci?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you know that Bosko Dragicevic and the police were looking for you whilst you were in opstina Prijedor at this time?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: They came to my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you speak to other people who had worked with you at Trnopolje, other policemen, about this?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I mean, have you ever made a statement, for instance, saying -- I will read out a passage to you now -- that you heard from the aforementioned guards, who they are I do not know, and military policemen that Tadic had gone to his wife in Serbia and had not returned to Kozarac? Had you talked to guards that you had previously worked with about Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: It is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you explain then why someone at the court in Sarajevo should take a statement from you saying that?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I do not know about that, but it is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you talk to any of the guards? Did you associate with any of those guards that you used to work at in Trnopolje during this one and a half years that you were in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If the police and Bosko Dragicevic were looking for you, did they ever come close to catching you in that one and a half years?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever have to take action so as to avoid them if they were in the area that you were in?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I merely tried to keep away so that they would not see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But there you were working openly in the fields and travelling from wherever you were to Orlovci to work? Did people not know you were around?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: People knew that they were all refugees in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told us this morning that because of your work at Trnopolje you had got to a psychological state that you wanted to leave the camp and that you escaped from it and hid somewhere for 10 days, is that right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Have you ever told anyone in relation to those proceedings in Sarajevo that you left the camp at your own request?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Excuse me, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am reading now from a statement provided for me by the Prosecution and it says this: "I performed guard duty in the Trnopolje camp until 28th December 1992 when I left the place at my own request". You told them you wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, I left because I did not want to be in that camp any more. I could not take it any more and I could not take those injections that I was receiving any more, and to do what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you explain then in a statement signed by you, taken down by someone in relation to your proceedings in Sarajevo, why they should say something about you that was not true?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, where I gave the statements, they took them in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You even signed a certificate saying that everyone had treated you properly during this interview and you dictated the statement to them and that it contained everything that you said?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you remember saying that, that you left at your own request?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I left the camp by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, what I am suggesting to you is this, that you did not have these problems that you told us about, and you just left that camp and no one was bothered to hunt down or track you down so that you had to live in hiding because you were living quite openly. Do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said that you had not heard about Dusko Tadic on the television or in the news in Prijedor when you were there until July 1994, is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Everyone in opstina Prijedor knew of Dusko Tadic's arrest in Germany in 1994, did they not? Everyone was talking about it in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Where I was in that area, there was no electricity, I am sorry, and I do not read Vjesnik. I do not read the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, if you had talked to guards and military policemen who worked at Trnopolje with you, they would have known about that, would they not?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: With those policemen, I did not speak nor do I know whether they knew anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I mean, did you know that Dusko Tadic had gone to his wife in Serbia and had left Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were talking to people in Kozarac, were you not, who lived there?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You do not remember telling them that in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That you had heard from Kozarac inhabitants about Dusko Tadic? You do not remember saying that to them there in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I did not say that in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Or is that another thing that the clerk has made up? In July 1994 you told us that you joined the army and you would have been 18 years old then, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To be mobilized in the army, did you report to barracks in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No, in the military office in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you get a call-up notice telling you to report there?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, someone within the local administration for mobilization knew where you were living?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: They knew that I was a refugee and they knew the surrounding area where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This notice came from Prijedor, did it?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you went to the Prijedor office. Did you already have a military book?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I received a military book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you receive your military book?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: When I joined the army in Karlinovik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you had not had a military book when you went to Prijedor aged 16 in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In October 1992 when you went to those barracks in Prijedor, was that again as the result of a call-up notice? You told us you were under age.

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you served as a guard at Trnopolje camp, was that part of your mobilization?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, that was mobilization, that was to be on the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you served as a guard at Trnopolje camp as part of your mobilization, was that entered into any book or record?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What book or record was that?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: That was entered in the headquarters in Trnopolje where Dusko Tadic and Bosko Dragicevic were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, you have said that Dusko Tadic was the Commander of the camp at Trnopolje, have you not?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were describing both him and Dragicevic yesterday as being a Camp Commander instead of describing Tadic as the Camp Commander. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Because Dusko Tadic gave orders to do what should not have been done against these people that were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But Bosko Dragicevic you have described as the deputy Camp Commander, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes, deputy to Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who was the Camp Commander at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic was the main one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You never saw a man called Slobodan Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you remember when you gave your statement in Sarajevo describing Dusko Tadic as being clean shaven and short grey-ish hair?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Sorry, he was not grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you remember saying that though when you gave your statement in Sarajevo in ----

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic was -- had curly hair and he had receding hair and he was stock -- he was well built.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, you describe him as having receding hair, is that right?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Sorry, but those are the -- that is receding hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I mean, was there any reason why you changed the colour of his hair when you gave evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Every person can change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, but you were not describing someone changing in appearance. You were describing who they were when you said that you had dealings with them for three months in 1992. Did anyone tell you to give him a different colour hair?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because you said he had black hair that was curly with sideburns, did you not?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To say he had short grey-ish hair would be wrong to describe Dusko Tadic, would it not?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I know who Dusko Tadic is. I knew him a while ago when we worked in the camp and I know that he is sitting at the table and I know that that is Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you have seen him on television in Prijedor anyway, have you not, in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: People knew you well enough to be able to give you a call up notice to go to the military office in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you started work at the camp, you told us that you were to be paid money. How much was that to be?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: Around 300 deutschemarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you ever paid that money?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that a reason for you leaving the camp, the fact that you needed to support yourself and had to get a job somewhere?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You told the Court about Dusko Tadic's house. What town was that house in?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: It was in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said it was near a petrol station. Which petrol station was that? Can you identify it at all for us?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: His house is located near the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How would you get to the petrol station from his house?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: It depends whether you are going down Mount Kozara on the asphalt, then his -- you pass his house and then you reach the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can put Exhibit 196 in front of you? This is a plan of Kozarac that has been provided for the Court. If it could be put on the overhead projector? Perhaps if you turned your chair and with the telescopic marker if you could indicate for us the petrol station? The big thick black mark running across the map diagonally is Marsala Tita Street and also marked is the church with a cross, the mosque and the school down near the triangle in the centre of Kozarac. Can you mark the petrol station for us at all? If you do not recognise or you cannot familiarise yourself with the map, please say so.

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: This map is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. Are you able in any way to indicate where Dusko Tadic's house is on Marsala Tita Street?

utterances.speaker: OK
utterances.text: I do not know which street is called Marsala Tita but I know where -- I know where Kozarac is.
